trap.wrong: "Cache supplier prices for a few hours and use them for booking."
trap.why: Supplier prices and availability change constantly; booking at a cached price leads to failed bookings or selling at a loss, while querying suppliers live on every search is too slow and exceeds rate limits.
trap.probe: Tiered freshness: cached prices for search, live verification before booking, and handling price changes honestly.
trap.say: "Search uses cached prices with known freshness; when the user selects an option, we re-price live with the supplier; if it changed, we show the new price before payment; and caching is tuned by look-to-book ratio and supplier limits."

thesis: With external inventory, use different freshness for different steps: cached or precomputed prices for search, live re-pricing when the customer selects, and confirmation at booking. Communicate price changes before charging, and tune caching to supplier rate limits and look-to-book ratios.
pitch: In travel, millions of searches happen for every booking, the look-to-book ratio, and suppliers like airlines, hotel systems and global distribution systems are slow, rate-limited and charge per query. So search results come from a cache of recent prices, refreshed by a mix of what users actually search for and proactive refresh of popular routes and dates, each entry tagged with its age. Results show prices as 'from' or with a freshness indicator. When a user selects an option, the system re-prices it live with the supplier, which is fewer and more valuable calls; if the price or availability changed, the user sees that before entering payment, never after. At booking, the supplier confirms, ideally with a hold or the exact fare quote referenced. I'd monitor price accuracy, how often re-pricing differs from the cached price and by how much, per supplier and route, and use that to tune cache TTLs. Supplier calls go through a gateway with rate limiting, caching, timeouts and circuit breakers, since one slow supplier shouldn't slow all searches.

points.d: Searches vastly outnumber bookings; live supplier queries per search are too slow and expensive.
Store prices with timestamps; refresh popular items proactively and others on demand.
Verify price and availability with the supplier when the user picks an option.
Book against the verified quote, using supplier holds where available.
Show changes before payment, with clear messaging; never charge more than displayed.
Track cached vs live price differences per supplier and route to tune TTLs and refresh.
Rate limits, timeouts, circuit breakers and per-supplier isolation so one slow supplier doesn't degrade search.

decision: Cached prices for discovery, live verification for commitment, and transparent handling of differences; tune freshness per supplier using measured price accuracy.
numbers: Look-to-book example: 1,000 searches per booking. Live-querying a supplier for every search at 1 million searches a day means 1 million calls; caching with live re-pricing only on selection (say 5% of searches) cuts it to 50,000.
pitfalls: Booking at cached prices without re-pricing.
Showing a price change only after payment details are entered or charged.
Live supplier calls on every search.
One slow supplier blocking the entire results page.

followups.q: How do you rank results if some prices are stale?
followups.a: Use cached prices with freshness weighting, and prefer options with recently verified prices when quality matters.

followups.q: A supplier is down. What do users see?
followups.a: Results from that supplier marked unavailable or hidden, while other suppliers continue; cached prices aren't bookable until re-priced.

followups.q: How do you handle currency and taxes from suppliers?
followups.a: Normalise at the gateway, record supplier currency and conversion, and show final totals including taxes at re-price time.

example: A travel site booked hotels at prices cached for 6 hours and had 7% of bookings fail or lose money. Adding live re-pricing on room selection, showing changes before payment, and per-supplier TTLs tuned by accuracy data cut failures below 1%.
